To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the multihop logical ring topology is the best choice for small to medium size networks, while the multihop hypercube topology is the best for large networks.
the multihop logical ring and star topologies are the two most attractive regular logical network topologles, and that the multihops star topology is the best of the two in most performance metrics.

(1) the ring topology is best for small networks, the star topology is best for large networks, the mesh topology is best for medium-sized networks, the tree topology is best for hierarchical networks, and the bus topology is best for broadcast/multicast applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of efficient, scalable, and fault-tolerant regular logical topologies for optical networks.
the development of efficient and flexible regular logical topologies for WDM optical networks.
the development and performance evaluation of regular and irregular logical network topologies for light-wave networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no single regular topology can be the best for all applications.
no single logical topology is best suited for all types of networks and applications.
there is no single regular logical topology that is superior to the others for all performance metrics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a multihop logical ring is a good choice for small networks (less than 20 nodes), a logical bus is suitable for large networks (more than 20 nodes) and a logical mesh is a good choice if the network is expected to grow in size.
the logical topologies that provide a better network utilization also have a higher fault tolerance.
the regular topologies are more efficient than the arbitrary topologies for the same network size and degree of nodal connectivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the regular logical topology of a multihop optical network is not a simple function of the number of available optical wavelengths and the number of nodes, but it is also a function of the number and type of transceivers at each node.
the choice of the logical network topology is a function of the specific application requirements.
there is no "one-size-fits-all" regular topology that is best suited for all applications.
